newsitem.title: USA: EU issues formal objection to Boeing merger.
newsitem.headline: EU issues formal objection to Boeing merger.

text.p: The European Union's executive body Wednesday formally notified Boeing Co. that it objects to the aerospace giant's proposed acquisition of rival McDonnell Douglas Corp.
Boeing said in a statement it remains confident the planned $14 million merger will be completed this summer despite the objections from the European Commission.

The 40-page "statement of objections" came as no surprise after European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert repeatedly declared his opposition to the merger, citing recent exclusive sales deals negotiated by Boeing that have shut out Europe's Airbus Industrie consortium.

Boeing Chairman Phil Condit said the company would continue working with EU officials but reiterated Boeing's position that the U.S. Federal Trade Commission should have the main authority over whether the merger should be allowed.

"While the merger has raised a number of issues in the European Union, there is one fundamental antitrust issue: Does the combination of Boeing with McDonnell Douglas' commercial airplane unit have a restrictive effect on competition?" Condit said in a statement.
He said the answer is no because McDonnell Douglas' share of the commercial airplane market has fallen to 4 percent, while Europe's Airbus Industrie has seen its share rise to more than 30 percent.
In its statement, Boeing also responded to concern that its commercial aircraft operations benefit from the "spillover" of government-funded defence and space operations.
Condit said Boeing complies with a 1992 treaty between the United States and European Union that covers such subsidies.

A Boeing spokeswoman said the company would prepare a response to be delivered to the European Commission at a hearing June 12 and 13. The commission is expected to issue a final ruling on the merger by the end of July.

The European move came the same day a published report said Continental Airlines Inc. was poised to become the third major airline to sign an exclusive supplier arrangement with Boeing following similar deals with AMR Corp.'s American Airlines and Delta Air Lines Inc.

Boeing and Continental declined to comment on the report in The Wall Street Journal, which said the carrier would order 10 of Boeing's twin-engine 777 jets and 30 of the smaller 767s valued at a total $4 billion.
But Condit said the deals with American and Delta came only after aggressive competition with Airbus.
Boeing stock rose $2.50 to $102.50 on the New York Stock Exchange, mainly on the Continental report, analysts said. News of the EU's objections came after the market closed.
Boeing also said Wednesday it will speed up production to a record 43 airplanes a month early next year from the current 29, reflecting continued strong demand.
Boeing previously had announced plans to increase production to 40 a month by the fourth quarter of this year, surpassing its previous record of 39.5 a month set in 1992.
Specifically Boeing said it would increase production of its 737, 747 and 757 models in the first quarter of 1998, while cutting production of its 777 to five a month from seven.
Production of the 737 will rise to 24 a month from 21, while production of the 747 and 757 will rise to five each from four.

Analyst Bill Whitlow of Safeco Corp. said the latest changes would have no material impact on 1998 revenues, although he estimated Boeing would deliver a record 495 planes next year, up from his previous estimate of 470.
Boeing reiterated it expects to deliver 340 jets this year, compared with 218 last year and a record 446 in 1992.
